To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) community members can be trained to measure species richness of fern communities in the Ecuador Amazon; (2) species richness estimates by community members are highly correlated to species richness estimates by trained biologists; and (3) community-based monitoring schemes can produce accurate data for local and regional environmental management.

we tested the accuracy of nonexperts in biodiversity monitoring using fern species richness and showed that with relatively little training communities can use costeffective methods to accurately measure biodiversity.

1) non-experts, with relatively little training in the use of visual guides, can accurately estimate fern species richness, 2) the use of visual aids can increase the accuracy of non-exerts and 3) non-experts can be trained to use visual aids to estimate fern species richness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a community-based monitoring system that can be used to measure changes in biodiversity.
the development of a simple and inexpensive method for the assessment of species richness of fern species by community-based monitoring schemes.
developing a community monitoring scheme that will enable local communities to contribute data on biodiversity to the conservation of their natural resources and to the scientific community.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data produced by community members using simple visual guides and hands on training is comparable to that produced by experienced field biologist and can be used to monitor changes in biodiversity.
the results obtained in this study suggest that the use of simple and cost-effective methods to teach local people to measure biodiversity can yield accurate data.
community-based monitoring is a viable alternative for biodiversity monitoring and can provide accurate information on species richness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, with the right training, community members can be taught to accurately measure species richness and that these data can be used in conservation planning.
non-experts can be taught to collect accurate biodiversity information.
the use of community-based monitoring is a viable and accurate alternative to the use of expert-based monitoring schemes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, with appropriate training, non-expert groups are capable of producing accurate and reliable data on biodiversity, which can be used to inform local management decisions.
community-based monitoring can be a useful tool to collect biodiversity data, and can help local communities to become more involved in environmental conservation.

community-based monitoring exercises can be a powerful tool to engage local people in the collection of biodiversity data, and to provide them with a platform to contribute to environmental management decisions.
